tracks.label: Opening
tracks.text: Chapter 1. What Makes a Bird a Bird. Walk outside almost anywhere on Earth, from a city sidewalk to an Antarctic beach, and within a few minutes you will probably see a dinosaur. It might be a pigeon on a ledge or a sparrow in a hedge. That is not a figure of speech. It is the conclusion of more than 150 years of fossil discoveries, beginning with a feathered skeleton found in a German quarry in 1861. To see why scientists are so confident of it, we first need to answer a plainer question: what, exactly, makes a bird a bird? The answer starts with something you can pick up on almost any walk, the feather. This chapter answers the question the rest of the course depends on: what is a bird? You will see that one trait, the feather, sets birds apart from every other living animal, and that much of a bird’s skeleton is built around flight. You will also learn where birds come from (they are the one surviving branch of the dinosaurs) and how scientists name and organize the roughly 11,000 species alive today. By the end you will have the vocabulary used in every later chapter, from flight in Chapter 2 to field identification in Chapter 4.

tracks.label: 1.1 Feathers: the defining trait
tracks.text: Section 1 point 1. Feathers: the defining trait. Many traits we associate with birds are shared with other animals. Bats and insects fly. Crocodiles and turtles lay eggs. Turtles have beaks. Only one trait belongs to birds alone among living animals: feathers. Every one of the roughly 11,000 living bird species has them, from the Bee Hummingbird of Cuba, which weighs about 2 grams, to the Common Ostrich, which can weigh more than 100 kilograms. If an animal alive today has feathers, it is a bird; if it lacks them, it is not. A feather is made of keratin, a tough structural protein. The main feather keratin, beta-keratin, is shared with reptile scales; your fingernails are made of a different type, alpha-keratin. Look at a large wing feather and you will see its basic plan. The hollow base, the calamus, sits in a follicle in the skin. It continues as the rachis, the central shaft. On each side of the rachis is a flat vane made of hundreds of side branches called barbs. The vane holds together because of a smaller level of branching. Each barb carries tiny branches of its own, the barbules. Barbules on one side of a barb have minute hooks; barbules on the other side are grooved. The hooks of one barb catch the grooves of the next barb, the way the teeth of a zipper lock together. When a feather is ruffled, the barbs separate. When the bird runs the feather through its bill, a behavior called preening, the hooks catch again and the vane is restored. Feathers come in several types. Contour feathers cover the body and give it its smooth outer shape. Flight feathers are the large, stiff feathers of the wing (the remiges) and the tail (the rectrices). Down feathers lie under the contour feathers; their barbules have no hooks, so they stay fluffy and trap warm air. Birds also have hair-like filoplumes, which sense the position of the other feathers, and stiff bristles around the eyes and mouth in birds such as nightjars and flycatchers. Feathers do far more than make flight possible. They insulate, and many birds waterproof them with oil from a preen gland at the base of the tail. They carry color: the red of a Northern Cardinal comes from carotenoid pigments the bird gets from its food, while the blue of a Blue Jay is a structural color, made by the way tiny structures inside the feather scatter light rather than by any blue pigment. Feathers also camouflage, signal to mates and rivals, and in some species make sound. Feathers wear out, so birds replace them in a process called molt. Most birds molt all their feathers at least once a year, usually a few at a time so they can still fly. The number of feathers varies enormously. Classic counts found about 940 contour feathers on a Ruby-throated Hummingbird and more than 25,000 on a Tundra Swan, most of the swan’s on its long neck and head. A common misconception: Feathers are just a fancy kind of hair. In fact, Feathers and hair evolved separately, in the dinosaur and mammal lineages, and are built from different proteins: feathers mainly from beta-keratin, hair from alpha-keratin. Hair is a single strand; feathers branch.

tracks.label: 1.2 The avian skeleton: built for flight
tracks.text: Section 1 point 2. The avian skeleton: built for flight. A bird’s skeleton has two jobs that pull in different directions: it must be strong enough to survive the forces of flapping and landing, and light enough to lift. Birds solve this partly by fusing bones that are separate in other animals. Fused bones make a rigid frame without heavy joints and ligaments. Four fusions are worth learning now: the furcula, or wishbone, made from the two collarbones; the carpometacarpus, made from hand bones; the synsacrum, made from fused lower back and front tail vertebrae, which is in turn fused to the hip bones; and the pygostyle, made from the last tail vertebrae, which anchors the tail feathers. The most striking bone in a flying bird is the breastbone, or sternum. It carries a deep ridge called the keel, which anchors the flight muscles. The large pectoralis muscle pulls the wing down on the power stroke. A second muscle, the supracoracoideus, lifts the wing; its tendon runs over the shoulder through a pulley-like opening, so a muscle on the chest can pull the wing upward. In strong fliers such as pigeons, the flight muscles make up a quarter or more of body weight. Ostriches and emus, which do not fly, have a flat sternum without a keel. Many bird bones are hollow and connect to the air sacs of the breathing system, which you will study in Chapter 3. Inside, thin bony struts brace the walls, like the cross-braces in a bridge. A common claim is that birds have unusually light skeletons. The full story is more interesting. Earlier studies showed that bird skeletons weigh about as much as mammal skeletons of the same body size. A 2010 study by Elizabeth Dumont explained why: bird bone is denser than the bone of similar-sized rodents, and slightly denser than bat bone. Birds get strength for their weight from bone shape and fusion, not from a lighter skeleton overall. The head shows the same theme. Birds have no teeth. Their jaws are covered by a beak made of a keratin sheath over bone, which keeps growing throughout life and whose shape is adapted to diet, from the hooked bill of a hawk to the cone of a seed-eating finch. Losing teeth and heavy jaw muscles moves weight away from the front of the body; much of the grinding work is done instead by a muscular stomach, the gizzard, which sits near the bird’s center of gravity. A bird’s neck is long and flexible. Almost all mammals, giraffes included, have seven neck vertebrae; birds have between about 10 and 26, and swans have the most. The legs hold a surprise as well. Birds walk on their toes. The joint you see bending backward halfway down a bird’s leg is its ankle, not its knee. The real knee is tucked up against the body under the feathers, and the long bone below the ankle, the tarsometatarsus, is made of fused foot bones. A common misconception: Birds have hollow bones, so their skeletons weigh almost nothing. In fact, Many bird bones are hollow, but bird bone is dense, and a bird’s skeleton weighs about as much as a mammal skeleton of the same body size. The advantage comes from shape and fusion, not from a lighter skeleton.

tracks.label: 1.3 Birds are dinosaurs
tracks.text: Section 1 point 3. Birds are dinosaurs. Birds are dinosaurs. This is not a figure of speech. Biologists group living things by ancestry: a group includes a common ancestor and all of its descendants. Birds descend from a group of two-legged, mostly meat-eating dinosaurs called theropods, the same group that includes Tyrannosaurus and Velociraptor. So birds belong inside the dinosaurs, in the same way that bats belong inside the mammals even though they fly. Scientists call the extinct dinosaurs that were not birds non-avian dinosaurs. The first strong evidence came early. In 1861, two years after Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, quarry workers in the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, Germany, found a fossil of an animal about the size of a raven. It had feathered wings and a wishbone like a bird, but also teeth, clawed fingers, and a long bony tail like a small dinosaur. It was named Archaeopteryx and is about 150 million years old, from the Late Jurassic period. For more than a century, Archaeopteryx was the main fossil linking feathers to dinosaurs. That changed in 1996, when a farmer in Liaoning Province, China, found Sinosauropteryx, a small theropod about 125 million years old, covered in simple filament-like feathers. It was clearly not a bird, yet it had feathers. Since then, dozens of feathered dinosaurs have been found, including Microraptor, which had long feathers on both its arms and its legs, and Yutyrannus, a relative of Tyrannosaurus about 9 meters long with a coat of filaments. Microscopic pigment structures preserved in some fossils even let researchers reconstruct color; Sinosauropteryx had a reddish-brown tail with pale rings. These fossils show that feathers came before flight. The earliest feathers were simple filaments, probably useful for warmth and display. Over millions of years they became branched, then formed flat vanes, and only later were large vaned feathers on the arms used to glide and fly. When you see a feather on a bird today, you are looking at a structure that is older than birds themselves. About 66 million years ago, an asteroid roughly 10 kilometers wide struck what is now the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. The impact and its aftermath ended the non-avian dinosaurs, along with a large share of the species on Earth. Some birds survived. Research suggests the surviving bird lineages were mostly ground-dwelling. Their descendants spread rapidly into the space left behind, and most major groups of modern birds appeared within a few million to roughly 15 million years. Every bird you see today is a member of that surviving branch. A common misconception: Birds evolved from pterosaurs, the flying reptiles. In fact, Pterosaurs were close relatives of the dinosaurs but not dinosaurs. They evolved flight on their own and died out 66 million years ago with no descendants. Birds descend from theropod dinosaurs.

tracks.label: 1.4 How many birds, and how we name them
tracks.text: Section 1 point 4. How many birds, and how we name them. Scientists recognize about 11,000 species of birds. The exact number depends on which list you use, because experts sometimes disagree about whether two populations are one species or two. When a species is divided into two, it is called a split; when two are combined, a lump. The number of individual birds is far larger. One 2021 study estimated about 50 billion birds alive on Earth, though estimates like this are uncertain. To avoid confusion, every species has a two-part scientific name, a system the Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus applied consistently to animals in 1758, the official starting point for zoological names. The first part is the genus, written with a capital letter; the second is the specific name, written in lowercase. Both are written in italics. The American Robin is Turdus migratorius: Turdus is Latin for thrush, and migratorius means migratory. Scientific names solve a real problem. Common names change from place to place. In Britain, “robin” means the European Robin, Erithacus rubecula, a small orange-breasted bird in a different family from the American Robin. The two birds were given the same common name by English settlers who were reminded of the robin at home, but their scientific names show at once that they are different birds, in different genera and, it turns out, different families. Species are grouped into a nested hierarchy. Birds make up the class Aves. The class is divided into orders, whose names end in -iformes; orders into families, whose names end in -idae; families into genera; and genera into species. The American Robin sits in order Passeriformes, family Turdidae, genus Turdus. The Passeriformes, often called perching birds (most of them are songbirds), are the largest order: about 60 percent of all bird species belong to it. In North America, official English names are set by the American Ornithological Society, and they are capitalized (American Robin) to show that they are the name of one species, not a description. In 2023 the society announced that it would change the English names of birds in its region that are named after people. For a beginner, the most useful step is to learn families first. Once you can tell that a bird is a thrush, a warbler or a woodpecker, you have narrowed thousands of possibilities to a handful, which is exactly how field guides and the identification methods in Chapter 4 work. A common misconception: Once a species has a scientific name, the name never changes. In fact, Scientific names change when new evidence, often DNA, shows that a species belongs in a different genus, or when species are split or lumped. The naming rules keep every name unique and traceable, not permanent.
